## How the teams were graded {#method}

Nine teams, one per AI provider, each on that provider's own agent harness, carried out the internship subject autonomously, with the same budgets and time limit. Four criteria, known to the teams from the start, count equally:

- **Scientific quality** and **compliance with the subject's instructions**, graded from 0 to 100 by the jury on the evidence each team left (report, records, code, results).
- **Cost control**: 100 times the share of the two budgets left at delivery (model calls and GPU weigh alike).
- **Delivery time**: 100 times the share of the 1.5 hours left at delivery.

The jury's grades are **absolute**: the same scale for any research work, whatever its means. For scientific quality, 100 is a historic discovery that marks the discipline, 90 a landmark paper, 75 a strong publishable contribution, 60 a sound complete study (a workshop paper or a good master's thesis), 45 a good internship report, 30 a small pilot with some supported results, 15 preliminary runs, 5 scaffolding, 0 nothing. Compliance is the share of the subject's instructions met, a justified departure counting as not met. With 5 USD and 1.5 hours, low grades are expected; the means and the incidents are described for each team but do not move its grades.

Cost control and delivery time are measured by the race framework from its ledgers, and count 0 for a team that did not deliver; delivered teams rank before the others.

The jury graded **anonymously**: each team was known to it only by a pseudonym (Team A to Team I), every name of a provider, model or agent tool was removed from what it read, and it read nothing else. It graded against the means (the budgets, the time, a shared 4-core machine) and against each team's incidents, telling apart what was inside and outside the team's control. The jury was one judge: a claude-fable-5-2 agent.

## Team by team {#teams}

### 1. OpenAI {#openai}

OpenAI compared an unconstrained flow-matching model, a soft physics loss and post-sampling projection and energy-budget correction on an analytic heat equation and a very small 3D periodic MHD system, with three seeds and finite-sample floors. Projection gives exact divergence control, the soft MHD loss does not help, and the generated distributions and parameter response remain far from the reference. It is a clean, honest small pilot at toy resolution.

**Means.** Delivered after 0.33 h of 1.5 h, with 0.64 USD of model calls and 0.23 USD of GPU. Efficient, but more than an hour and most of both budgets were left unused; larger grids, more seeds or a design-level constraint were within reach.

**Context.** No incident. The scale of the study is the team's own choice.

**Strengths.**

- Reference-vs-reference floors next to every distributional metric
- Three training seeds with ranges, negative result reported
- Operator and convergence tests committed with outputs
- Careful statement of what the corrections do and do not prove

**Weaknesses.**

- 8^3 grid with 5 modes per direction: not turbulence, not a dynamo
- No constraint by model design
- Generated distributions remain several times above the floor; weak conditioning
- Topology and helicity are coarse proxies; no figures

### 2. DeepSeek {#deepseek}

DeepSeek trained conditional flow matching in a PCA latent on a 2D MHD solver dataset and a Burgers benchmark, comparing an unconstrained model, a stream-function design and a physics-informed loss against a truncation floor. The divergence-free design is exact and near the floor on energy balance, while the physics loss does not improve distributions and its claimed benefit on parameter response rests on one seed and unequal training. A well-documented 2D pilot, limited by confounded comparisons and small scale.

**Means.** 0.28 USD of model calls, no GPU, delivered at 1.15 h. Frugal and CPU-only by choice; the unused GPU budget could have paid for equal seeds and step counts across variants.

**Context.** The model substitution has no visible effect on the work; the Hub failure left dataset and weights staged locally instead of published.

**Strengths.**

- Truncation floor and reference floors reported next to model values
- Held-out and interpolation parameter grids, significance tests
- Two benchmarks with a real 2D MHD solver
- Rejected designs and an evaluation-path bug are logged

**Weaknesses.**

- Raw vs structural comparison confounded by representation; phys vs struct by training length
- 2D, low Re/Rm, 256 training fields, MLP on 32 PCA modes
- Key conditioning claim from a single seed
- Stale figures in the compliance and decision records; no sampling-time constraint measured

### 3. Anthropic {#anthropic}

Anthropic built a 2D pseudo-spectral MHD dataset and compared five ways of enforcing zero divergence in conditional flow matching, with a data noise floor and a held-out parameter band. Hard constraints reach round-off divergence and the stream-function model has the best spectra, but every model is a 400-step single-seed CPU run far from the floor. An honest, under-trained 2D pilot shaped by the loss of GPU access.

**Means.** 1.53 USD of model calls, no GPU spend, delivered at 1.31 h. The GPU budget could not be used because of the proxy incident; the CPU fallback was handled sensibly but a 1500-step batch was abandoned.

**Context.** No GPU training; the reported models are 400-step single-seed CPU runs instead of longer multi-seed ones.

**Strengths.**

- Real 2D MHD data over a continuous parameter range with a held-out band
- Five strategies including in-loop projection and a projection layer
- Noise floor reported; status line states the limits bluntly
- A bug that made M1 identical to M0 was caught and disclosed

**Weaknesses.**

- Single seed, 400 steps, far from the floor
- No simple PDE stage, no 3D, no helicity
- Solver validation not evidenced
- Nothing published; references not read

### 4. Alibaba {#alibaba}

Alibaba built a validated spectral toolkit for the kinematic ABC induction problem and compared six constraint and prior strategies for conditional flow matching on 16^3 fields. The comparison comes from 120 training steps on 48 fields with one seed, so only the by-construction divergence results are firm, and the report still contains empty tables and inconsistent numbers. Ambitious design, preliminary evidence.

**Means.** 0.52 USD of model calls and 0.31 USD of GPU that produced no computation; delivered at 1.41 h. Twenty minutes went to a crash-looping pod and much of the rest to dataset rebuilds, leaving 22 seconds of training for the reported study.

**Context.** The study fell back to CPU and to a reduced-capacity run; the planned benchmarks, guidance arm and resolution study were not produced.

**Strengths.**

- Validation suite of exact identities that caught real bugs
- Four constraint routes plus a prior arm in one code path
- 3D induction with Rm held out
- Limits and the re-scoping are logged in detail

**Weaknesses.**

- 120 training steps, one seed, 12 test fields
- No growing dynamo in the sampled range; amplitude normalised away
- Report unfinished and internally inconsistent
- Simple benchmarks and several promised analyses not run

### 5. Moonshot {#moonshot}

Moonshot generated a 2D Kolmogorov-flow dataset over four Reynolds numbers and compared an unconstrained flow-matching U-Net with a divergence penalty, a stream-function design and a Helmholtz projection at sampling. Projection gives exact divergence at little cost, the penalty is a poor trade-off, and the stream-function model failed at this budget. The work is a sound single-seed first stage that never reaches MHD, 3D, helicity or topology.

**Means.** 4.35 USD of 5 USD of model calls for a study with no sub-agents, 0.54 USD of GPU, delivered at 1.04 h. The GPU was used well after a slow first pod; the model budget was nearly exhausted by the harness alone.

**Context.** About ten minutes lost to GPU provisioning and a slow pod; no visible effect on the content otherwise.

**Strengths.**

- Real forced-flow dataset over a wide Re range with a properly sized model
- All three constraint routes under one protocol
- Matched/mismatched conditioning test
- Negative result on the design route reported

**Weaknesses.**

- No MHD at all, 2D only
- Single seed, temporally correlated train/test split
- No helicity, topology or energy-budget metric
- Records inconsistent with the report on training settings

### 6. Zhipu {#zhipu}

Zhipu planned a four-way comparison of constraint injection on 2D Kolmogorov flow and a synthetic 3D solenoidal field family. Only the 2D evaluation finished, on an under-fit model where sampling constraints made things worse, and the 3D models were trained but never evaluated. The repository supports very few of the report's statements.

**Means.** 2.33 USD of model calls and 1.13 USD of GPU, delivered at 1.36 h. The GPU ran for the whole session but three evaluation restarts and a 4 KB transfer channel meant almost none of its output reached the repository.

**Context.** The session cut cost context and time in the last 50 minutes, and the transfer limit kept checkpoints, figures and metrics off the repository; the 3D evaluation did not exist at delivery.

**Strengths.**

- Clear framing of where a constraint can enter
- Forced 2D turbulence benchmark with a held-out Re
- Negative 2D result reported rather than hidden
- Delivery cut stated openly in the report

**Weaknesses.**

- Core 3D study has no results
- Cited result files are missing
- Under-fit 2D model, single seed
- Conclusions exceed the evidence; nothing published

### 7. xAI {#xai}

xAI did not deliver; its repository holds a report and results for Burgers and for 2D and 3D kinematic induction with conditional rectified flows and constraints by design, loss and sampling. Conditioning helps on Burgers and projection reduces divergence, but the MHD models barely learn their fields and rest on a handful of samples and one seed. The report is exemplary in honesty and thin in established results.

**Means.** 4.80 USD of 5 USD of model calls, no GPU, not delivered. The team let its contexts grow to about 200 thousand tokens per call and exhausted the model budget in about 20 minutes of metered work, leaving most of the time unused.

**Context.** The restart and the cost-rule stop cost a few minutes; the absence of delivery comes mainly from the team's own model spend. Graded on what the repository holds.

**Strengths.**

- Strict separation of measured, published and conjectured
- Negative results kept (2D design route, single-seed ranking withdrawn)
- Three benchmarks including 3D with helicity
- Exact Burgers reference and physics checks

**Weaknesses.**

- Tiny data and training; models near rel L2 = 1
- Four test fields per MHD table, one seed
- Kinematic, t_end 0.03: no dynamo dynamics
- Not delivered

### 8. Google {#google}

Google did not deliver: three incidents outside its control left it about twenty minutes of work, after which its provider refused every call. The repository contains a decisions log and untested package code, with no experiment, result or report. Nothing is established.

**Means.** 3.18 USD of model calls over 20 sessions and about 20 minutes of effective work before the provider account ran dry; no GPU. The time available went into writing a large package before any experiment.

**Context.** The team had roughly 20 minutes of working time and could neither run experiments nor deliver. Graded on what the repository holds, which is code only.

**Strengths.**

- Broad, structured package layout covering the subject's stages
- Requirement extraction planned from the first minutes

**Weaknesses.**

- No run, no result, no report
- Synthetic hand-built 'dynamo' data instead of a solver
- Plan far larger than the window allowed

### 9. Mistral {#mistral}

Not graded: the provider account refused every call of the team (a rate limit of the account), so the team never worked.

## How close the calls are {#close}

- **A vs F (31 vs 30)** is the closest call and could go either way. F has more apparatus (floors, tests, figures, two grids); A has cleaner controls (equal budgets, three seeds everywhere) and a 3D nonlinear MHD system, at a far smaller resolution. I put A first because F's two main comparisons are confounded by representation and training length.
- **G vs D (26 vs 23)** is close. G's model is properly trained on turbulent data, but it never touches MHD; D addresses the subject's object (parametric MHD, topology metric) with models too under-trained to trust. On compliance D is ahead of G (43 vs 40). A judge who weighs the subject's MHD target more heavily could invert them.
- **I vs B (18 vs 17)** is a near tie. Both rest on barely trained models and a handful of test fields. I has three benchmarks, multi-seed Burgers and a consistent report; B has a better-validated toolkit and four routes on 16³ fields but an unfinished, inconsistent report. I did not deliver, which the framework scores separately.
- **The gaps F to G, D to I, B to C and C to H** are clear: each step loses either seeds and floors, or trained models, or the evaluation itself.
- All grades sit between 3 and 31 on science. None of the works reaches the level of a good internship report (45): the best are small pilots at toy resolution.
- I read every report and record in full and the code and result summaries that back the tables; the long raw JSON dumps and some code files were checked selectively against the reported numbers, not line by line.

## Limits of this grading {#limits}

- One judge, and it is an Anthropic model: the Anthropic team was graded, anonymously, by a model of its own provider.
- The judge read every report and record in full, and checked the long raw result files and some code files selectively against the reported numbers.
- With equal weights, the measured cost control and delivery time weigh as much as the two judged criteria: a team that delivered early and cheaply gains much on them, whatever its science.
- Delivery time is measured as it is: it does not discount the time a team lost to an incident outside its control (the Anthropic team lost about 25 minutes to a failure of the race framework).
- The reports were graded as the teams wrote them; the versions on this site were edited afterwards to remove file paths.

The jury's records (grades, the judge's ranking, the facts measured) are in the repository's [research/race-2026-11-15/jury](https://github.com/knoel99/milady-2027/tree/main/research/race-2026-11-15/jury).
